problem: VLM-based VLN models are evaluated only by closed-loop success rate, so it is unknown whether they ground actions in relevant semantic cues, use visual/text memory to track progress, or retain VLM concepts after fine-tuning. Interpretability work exists for older VLN models and for VLAs on manipulation, but not for VLM-based VLNs.
motivation: Success rate alone cannot show whether a model uses landmarks, shortcuts, or compensates via another modality. Failures may come from unused rather than missing concepts, so steering internal representations could fix behavior without retraining.
key_idea: Combine intervention-based attribution (ISS, IG, TAM) with activation/value-vector steering to characterize what four VLM-based VLN policies rely on, then use a simulation-derived activation vector to induce reasoning zero-shot on a real robot.
insight: The policies are sensitive to all modalities (current image, visual memory, instruction, text memory), with no single dominant one and no clear link between sensitivity and success. Robustness depends on the ability to recover via other modalities (e.g., CorrectNav is most robust to memory blurring despite high sensitivity). ISS and IG precision only reaches about 40-60%, so sensitivity extends to human-irrelevant regions, suggesting shortcuts or limited data diversity. VLM semantic concepts survive fine-tuning and can be steered, and a mean-difference vector raises reasoning frequency from 3% to 100%, whereas random vectors do not.
method: Interventional Significance Score (ISS): perturbs token groups (blur image regions, delete words, or replace them with antonyms) and scores each token by the divergence in the predicted trajectory (MSE of end-points plus a weighted angular difference).

Integrated Gradients and TAM baselines: IG integrates gradients of the mean log-likelihood of the generated action tokens from a corrupted to the original embedding; TAM uses the LM-head logit activation per input token with autoregressive-context removal.

Memory sensitivity and robustness probes: blur the oldest p% of memory images, or substitute the instruction with antonyms cumulatively, along ground-truth trajectories. Closed-loop SR is measured under blur levels.

Value-vector semantic steering: find FFN down-projection value vectors whose top-K vocabulary tokens match a concept (forward/turn, left/right) and clamp their activations to β (positive/negative sets).
Activation steering: take the mean-difference vector between positive (reasoning) and negative (direct action) hidden states at a layer and add α·d to the first output token.
Evaluation protocol: precision@k against manual annotations (200 open-loop image points, 100 text samples) on CorrectNav, DualVLN, AwareVLN and NaVILA, using R2R-CE val-unseen subsets.

setting.backbone: CorrectNav, DualVLN, AwareVLN, NaVILA (Qwen2.5-VL-based VLN policies, fine-tuned by their authors; analyzed, not retrained)
setting.training_data: none for this paper (pretrained VLN checkpoints analyzed; steering vectors computed from simulation activations, no weight updates)
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB with visual memory history and language instruction
setting.privileged: ground-truth trajectories used for sensitivity analyses; a human operator identifies failures and triggers steering in real-world tests

numbers_note: This is an analysis paper, not a benchmark-leaderboard paper. The SR values are from the authors' reproduction of baselines under blurring on an unspecified R2R-CE val-unseen subset; other results are precision, ISS, and steering statistics.
results: ISS gives better annotation alignment than IG (P@1 up to 0.66 for CorrectNav), but all precisions are about 40-60%. Semantic concepts persist in DualVLN, and neuron clamping shifts motion tokens (e.g., forward+/turn- gives -19.3% Left). Mean-vector steering raises AwareVLN's reasoning frequency from 3% to 100% at α=4, and in the real world raises SR from 37.2% to 74.4% (59.3% recovery from failure).
limitations: Steering requires an operator to detect failures and trigger it; no online, introspective trigger.

Small-scale evaluations (5 episodes for clamping, 12 episodes for memory analyses, 40 real trials, manual annotations on 100-200 points) and different camera/step configurations per baseline limit comparability.
Attribution shows sensitivity, not necessarily correctness, and text-sensitivity patterns are brittle and unexplained (e.g., AwareVLN's unstable end-of-trajectory behavior).
